title: Sahih Muslim 132a: That is the faith manifest
label: Hadith reference
note: Sahih Muslim 132a, in Sahih Muslim (sahih). Cited for: companions troubled by thoughts too grave to speak were told, 'That is the faith manifest'; such thoughts are a sign of faith, not a loss of it (Book of Faith, chapter on waswasah).

title: Sahih al-Bukhari 2528: Whispers of the heart are forgiven
label: Hadith reference
note: Sahih al-Bukhari 2528, in Sahih al-Bukhari (sahih). Cited for: Allah has forgiven the believers the thoughts that occur to their minds as long as they do not act on them or say them.

title: Sahih al-Bukhari 3276: Seek refuge and give up the thought
label: Hadith reference
note: Sahih al-Bukhari 3276, in Sahih al-Bukhari (sahih). Cited for: when Satan whispers 'Who created your Lord?', the believer seeks refuge with Allah and gives up such thoughts.

title: Quran 16:106: Forced words and a heart secure in faith
label: Quran source
note: Cited for: someone forced to say words of disbelief while their heart is secure in faith is excused; leaving faith means willingly opening the heart to disbelief. The English wording is a translation of the meaning (Saheeh International).

title: Misgivings Regarding Apostasy and How to Deal with Them
label: Scholar answer
note: Dr. Asim Yusuf, scholar and psychiatrist, 6 May 2014. Supports: blasphemous thoughts, slips of the tongue and unwitting statements do not take a person out of Islam ('You can't trip up and stumble out of the religion by mistake; you really have to try!'); 'A person who fears not being Muslim is by definition a Muslim'; severe doubts can be a medical or psychological problem, so do not be afraid to seek professional help.

title: How Can I Overcome Doubts and Whispers Regarding My Faith?
label: Scholar answer
note: Dr. Muhammad Fayez Awad, 20 February 2025. Supports: the difference between doubt and whispers (waswas); whispers are not contradictory to faith and do not take a person out of Islam; remedies include dua, daily remembrance, seeking refuge in Allah, ignoring the whispers and keeping good company.

title: Faith and Certainty (In Pursuit of Conviction, part 1)
label: Research education
note: Dr. Zohair Abdul-Rahman, published 13 June 2019, updated 22 July 2024. Supports (section 'Certainty as a spiritual pursuit'): 'Having uncomfortable thoughts or feelings that come to our mind does not contradict yaqeen or our faith', and the prophetic guidance to say 'I have faith in Allah', seek refuge and stop. The address redirects to yaqeeninstitute.ca from Canada.

title: Overcoming Intrusive Thoughts and Religious OCD: Prophetic Guidance on Moral Scrupulosity
label: Research education
note: Dr. Jibran Khokhar, published 13 August 2026. Supports (sections 'The Prophetic Principle: Thoughts Are Not Sins' and 'Divine Mercy and the Limits of Accountability'): thoughts are not sins, and when scrupulosity seriously interferes with worship, relationships and daily life, seeing a qualified mental health professional 'is not a sign of weak faith but a means of healing'.

title: Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder
organization: Centre for Addiction and Mental Health (CAMH)
label: Clinical information
note: CAMH, Toronto. Supports: common OCD obsessions include 'preoccupation with religious images and thoughts or fear of having blasphemous thoughts' and repeated doubting; compulsions include mental rituals such as praying; treatment ideally combines counselling (most often cognitive behavioural therapy) with medication. Review date not shown on the page.

title: Should a Convert Do His Shahada Publicly?
label: Scholar answer
note: Ustadha Shireen Ahmed, 16 January 2017. Supports: a public Shahada lets the community know you are Muslim, for example so that it knows to bury you as a Muslim. The teacher writes, 'I have heard it is better to say the shahada publicly, (even with just a few people) but if it is causing you any kind of anxiety it is not strictly necessary.' The 'better' part is her hedged report, not a ruling.

title: Shahada Online
label: Scholar answer
note: Shaykh Abdurragmaan Khan, checked by Shaykh Faraz Rabbani, 5 June 2020. Supports: a Shahada said through an online facility is valid; repeating it with a local imam is not incumbent but 'undoubtedly desired'; attach yourself to a local community and introduce yourself to one of its leaders. One answer; scholarly review is still needed.

title: Do I Need to Say 'Ashhadu' When Converting to Islam?
label: Scholar answer
note: Imam Yama Niazi, checked by Shaykh Faraz Rabbani, 12 March 2021. Supports: it is more cautious to say 'ashhadu' (I bear witness), but it is also acceptable if the Shahada is said without it.

title: Can I Marry a Woman Who Wants to Convert to Islam Because She Loves Me?
label: Scholar answer
note: Ustadha Shazia Ahmad, checked by Shaykh Faraz Rabbani, 14 August 2022. Supports: 'Marriage being the motivating factor is not a problem'; the person must sincerely believe: 'If she doesn't fundamentally believe in it, she should not say she does'; advises about a year of learning before marriage.

title: Is My Marriage Valid If My Husband Converted Only for Marriage?
label: Scholar answer
note: Mawlana Ilyas Patel, checked by Shaykh Abdul-Rahim Reasat, 22 March 2025. Supports: 'Conversion must be sincere'; questions about whether a marriage is valid go to a local imam. Cited only for the sincerity point and the referral; the site does not repeat the answer's ruling on a particular marriage.

title: Sunan an-Nasa'i 3341: Umm Sulaym, whose dowry was his Islam
label: Hadith reference
note: Sunan an-Nasa'i 3341, graded Hasan (Darussalam). Cited for: Abu Talhah proposed to Umm Sulaym and became Muslim, and she accepted his Islam as her dowry.

title: Owning or Gifting Books on Other Religions
label: Scholar answer
note: Ustadh Farid Dingle, checked by Shaykh Faraz Rabbani, 22 April 2021. Supports: owning books of other religions is not sinful in itself; the concern is only if reading them is likely to lead to disbelief; borrowed or institutional copies must be returned.

title: What is the Ruling of Reading the Jewish and Christian Bible?
label: Scholar answer
note: Shaykh Abdul-Rahim Reasat, checked by Shaykh Faraz Rabbani, 1 January 2024. Supports: reading the Bible may be permissible for someone who understands their own creed well and is not prone to doubts or confusion; 'Don't go online trying to find issues'. The answer's polemical reading list is not used on this site.

title: Quran 6:108: Do not insult what others worship
label: Quran source
note: Cited for: Muslims do not insult what other people call on besides Allah, so a new Muslim treats family religious items and practices with respect. The English wording is a translation of the meaning (Saheeh International).

title: Is It Permissible for a Muslim to Permanently Stay at a House Containing Hindu Idols? [Shafi'i]
label: Scholar answer
note: Shaykh Jamir Meah, 28 December 2016. Supports: a Shafi'i answer about a temporary stay (a year or two) in a friend's home where the main objects had been put away. Staying in a room with statues of animate beings is disliked in the reliable Shafi'i view, and another Shafi'i view says it is impermissible; it is permissible without dislike if they are elsewhere in the building; 'as a general rule, it is always better for a Muslim to stay clear'. It is not a ruling about living in a family home with a shrine.

title: Can Mistakenly Received Prasad Be Given to a Poor Non-Muslim or Must It Be Discarded?
label: Scholar answer
note: Mawlana Ilyas Patel, checked by Shaykh Abdul-Rahim Reasat, 22 December 2024. Supports: food offered at a temple in the name of other than Allah is not eaten (Hanafi reasoning from Mufti Shafi's Ma'arif al-Quran); if received by mistake it may be given to a non-Muslim; decline respectfully and keep relations peaceful.

title: Does the Concept of Karma Exist in Islam?
label: Scholar answer
note: Ustadh Abdullah Anik Misra, checked by Faraz Rabbani, 15 November 2012. Supports: Islam affirms that deeds have consequences but rejects reincarnation and an impersonal karma system; all outcomes are from Allah. The page cites the verse as 100:7-8; the correct reference is 99:7-8, which this site cites from Quran.com.

title: Quran 99:7-8: An atom's weight of good or evil
label: Quran source
note: Cited for: whoever does an atom's weight of good will see it, and whoever does an atom's weight of evil will see it; deeds have consequences, answered to Allah. The English wording is a translation of the meaning (Saheeh International).

title: What is the Ruling of Yoga?
label: Scholar answer
note: Shaykh Faraz Rabbani, 25 December 2012. Supports: 'When yoga is practiced purely for the element of physical exercise, then there is no harm in it'; its meditative and spiritual elements are avoided.

title: Is It Permissible for Muslims to Participate in Smudging?
label: Scholar answer
note: Shaykh Irshaad Sedick, checked by Shaykh Mohammad Abu Bakr Badhib, 13 April 2025. Supports: burning sage for fragrance or health is permissible; smudging done with the belief that it gives spiritual protection or connects to unseen forces conflicts with reliance on Allah and is avoided. Not written with Canadian Indigenous communities in mind.

title: Sahih al-Bukhari 1385: Every child is born on the fitrah
label: Hadith reference
note: Sahih al-Bukhari 1385, in Sahih al-Bukhari (sahih). Cited for: every child is born on the fitrah (natural disposition), and the parents raise the child into another religion.

title: Quran 30:30: The fitrah of Allah
label: Quran source
note: Cited for: the fitrah of Allah upon which He created all people. The English wording is a translation of the meaning (Saheeh International).

title: Can I Attend an Hindu Ceremony?
label: Scholar answer
note: Shaykh Farid Dingle, 10 October 2018. Supports: about a school cultural visit to a Diwali event at a temple: taking part in another religion's rite is not allowed, and the default is not to enter a church or temple without pressing need, although the answer notes 'reliable positions that permit one to enter churches or temples'. It does not address a family Diwali meal, gifts or sweets.

title: Can Muslims celebrate Chinese New Year?
organization: MuslimSG (Islamic Religious Council of Singapore, MUIS)
label: Religious authority platform
note: Article on MUIS's MuslimSG platform, updated 17 February 2026. Supports: reunion dinners, visiting elders, exchanging oranges, yusheng and red envelopes (ang bao) are cultural; citing Singapore's Office of the Mufti, one may attend a function with religious elements to observe and show respect without joining the ritual activities. note: Cited for: discuss with Jews and Christians only in the best way, and say 'our God and your God is one'. The English wording is a translation of the meaning (Saheeh International).

label: Hadith reference

label: Hadith reference

title: Sahih al-Bukhari 3448: The return of Jesus

note: Sahih al-Bukhari 3448, in Sahih al-Bukhari (sahih). Cited for: Jesus son of Mary will descend and judge justly.

label: Hadith reference

title: Sahih al-Bukhari 69: Make things easy
label: Hadith reference
note: Sahih al-Bukhari 69, in Sahih al-Bukhari (sahih). Cited for: 'Facilitate things to people', do not make things hard for them, and do not drive them away.

label: Hadith reference
note: Sahih al-Bukhari 1, in Sahih al-Bukhari (sahih). Cited for: deeds are rewarded according to their intentions. Cited only for intention as the heart of every act, not as reassurance about converting for marriage.

label: Hadith reference
note: Sahih al-Bukhari 56, in Sahih al-Bukhari (sahih). Cited for: whatever you spend for Allah's sake is rewarded, even a morsel you put in your wife's mouth; ordinary acts can be worship.

label: Quran source
note: Cited for: if you avoid the major sins you are forbidden, Allah will remove your lesser sins; sins are not all equal. The English wording is a translation of the meaning (Saheeh International).

label: Hadith reference
note: Sahih al-Bukhari 6857, in Sahih al-Bukhari (sahih). Cited for: the Prophet named seven great destructive sins, among them associating partners with Allah, sorcery and unlawful killing.

label: Hadith reference
note: Sahih al-Bukhari 7405, in Sahih al-Bukhari (sahih). Cited for: a hadith qudsi: 'I am just as My slave thinks I am'; supports holding hope in Allah.

title: Jami at-Tirmidhi 3540: Forgiveness as great as the earth
label: Hadith reference
note: Jami at-Tirmidhi 3540, graded Hasan (Darussalam). Cited for: a hadith qudsi: if you came with sins nearly as great as the earth, not associating anything with Allah, He would meet you with forgiveness nearly as great; hope alongside fear.

title: Quran 7:156: My mercy encompasses all things
label: Quran source
note: Cited for: Allah's mercy encompasses all things. The English wording is a translation of the meaning (Saheeh International).

title: Am I a Convert or a Revert?
label: Convert perspective
note: Kyle Abdur-Raqeeb MacPhail, 19 November 2015. An opinion piece: the author says 'So I am a convert not a revert', because becoming Muslim was a conscious choice, and argues that 'revert' suggests going backwards. Cited only to show that Muslims who came to Islam as adults use both words; it does not say either word is wrong for others.

title: What is a Madhhab? Exploring the Role of Islamic Schools of Law
label: Scholarly source
note: Published 31 December 2020, updated 22 July 2024. Supports: a school of law (madhhab) is a shared method of interpretation; the four Sunni schools (Hanafi, Maliki, Shafi'i, Hanbali) agree on foundations and differ on secondary matters; it presents following a recognised school as the normal way for a layperson to follow scripture.

title: Difference of Opinion: Where Do We Draw the Line?
label: Scholarly source
note: Published 10 December 2019, updated 22 July 2024. Supports: valid differences exist only on questions open to interpretation, and it gives five conditions for a valid opinion; a layperson needs a trustworthy teacher they can ask; declaring someone a disbeliever (takfir) is only for trained scholars; valid differences do not license picking whatever suits one's desires.

title: The Three Points of the Amman Message
label: Scholarly source
note: Supports: point 1 recognises as Muslims the followers of the four Sunni schools, the Ja'fari and Zaydi Shia schools, the Ibadi and Zahiri (spelt Thahiri on the page) schools, and says followers of Ash'ari creed, genuine Sufism (tasawwuf) and true Salafi thought may not be declared apostates; point 2 says disagreement on secondary matters is a mercy; point 3 says no one may issue a fatwa without personal qualifications and the methodology of the schools. Not every Sunni scholar accepts every detail.

title: The Qadianiya sect (Fatwa 4125)
label: Scholarly source
note: Cited only for the factual point that mainstream Sunni institutions hold Muhammad (peace be upon him) to be the last prophet (Quran 33:40) and place belief in a prophet after him outside Islam. The fatwa's own wording is polemical and is not used on this site.

title: Sahih al-Bukhari 7352: Two rewards for a judge who strives
label: Hadith reference

title: Quran 4:59: Refer disagreements to Allah and the Messenger
label: Quran source
note: Cited for: when believers disagree over anything, they refer it back to Allah and the Messenger. It is not cited for the idea that all differences are respected. The English wording is the Saheeh International translation of the meaning.

note: Cited for: Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah and the seal (last) of the prophets. The English wording is the Saheeh International translation of the meaning.

label: Hadith reference

title: Quran 49:13: Nations and tribes, to know one another

title: Islam and Anti-Blackness: Leaving Ignorance Behind

title: 'Not Quite Muslim Enough?': Black African Muslims and the Politics of Belonging in Muslim Spaces in Montreal, Canada
label: Academic study

title: Jinn and mental health: looking at jinn possession in modern psychiatric practice

title: What to do when someone dies
label: Public rights source
note: Updated 28 July 2026. title: Death investigations
organization: Government of Ontario (Office of the Chief Coroner)
label: Public rights source
note: Updated 21 September 2026. Supports: coroners investigate sudden and unexpected deaths; families should tell the coroner right away about religious or cultural needs around timing; the coroner considers the family's concerns, but the decision on an autopsy is legal and binding.

title: What to do when someone dies
label: Public rights source
note: Modified 18 September 2025. Supports: a federal checklist of steps after a death, notifying the government, benefits, and estates and wills.

title: Funeral and Burial

title: How to pray the funeral prayer (Salat al-Janazah) (IslamQA 12363)
label: Scholar answer

title: For Those Left Behind (video series)
label: Scholar answer

title: Reverted to Islam secretly and fears that her family will cremate her (Fatwa 92666)

title: Cremation, Interment and Funeral Services Act, sections 5 and 6
label: Public rights source
note: Supports, for British Columbia: section 5 gives the right to control disposition first to the personal representative named in the will, then the spouse, an adult child and others in order; section 6 makes a written preference in a will or preneed contract binding unless it is unreasonable, impracticable or a hardship.

title: Quran 2:156: To Allah we belong and to Him we return

organization: Yaqeen Institute (Najwa Awad and Sarah Sultan)
label: Scholar answer

title: Sahih al-Bukhari 1280: Mourning for three days
label: Hadith reference
note: In Sahih al-Bukhari (Book 23, Hadith 41): 'It is not legal for a woman who believes in Allah and the Last Day to mourn for more than three days for any dead person except her husband.' The wording is addressed to women, so scholars explain how it applies more widely.

title: The Fiqh (Jurisprudence) of Mourning
label: Scholar answer
note: Supports: mourning that pauses normal life is limited to three days, except for a widow, whose mourning of four months and ten days is required; Umm Salamah's prayer at a loss. The three-day hadith is Sahih al-Bukhari 1280.

title: Quran 2:234: The widow's waiting period
label: Quran source
note: Cited for: a widow observes a waiting period (iddah) of four months and ten days. The English wording is a translation of the meaning, from The Clear Quran (Dr. Mustafa Khattab), the Quran.com default.

title: Sahih Muslim 963a: A funeral prayer for the deceased
label: Hadith reference
note: In Sahih Muslim. The Prophet's prayer in a funeral prayer, beginning 'O Allah, forgive him and have mercy on him' (Allahumma ighfir lahu warhamhu).

title: Sahih Muslim 920a: The Prophet's prayer for Abu Salamah
label: Hadith reference
note: In Sahih Muslim. The Prophet's prayer for Abu Salamah after his death, asking Allah to forgive him, raise his rank and make his grave spacious and full of light.

title: Sunan Ibn Majah 1498: A funeral prayer dua
label: Hadith reference
note: In Sunan Ibn Majah, graded Hasan (Darussalam). A dua the Prophet said in the funeral prayer for the living and the dead among the Muslims.

title: Quran 17:24: A prayer for parents
label: Quran source
note: Cited for: the prayer 'My Lord, have mercy upon them as they raised me when I was young'. The English wording is a translation of the meaning, from The Clear Quran (Dr. Mustafa Khattab), the Quran.com default.

title: Hope and Healing: Supplications for a Loved One Who Passed Away
label: Scholar answer
note: Published 8 August 2024, updated 8 September 2026. Supports: duas for a Muslim who has died, from Sahih Muslim 963 and 920, Sunan Ibn Majah 1498 (Hasan) and Quran 17:24.

title: Coping with Grief: A Spiritual and Psychological Guide
organization: Yaqeen Institute (Sarah Sultan and Najwa Awad)
label: Scholar answer
note: Published 12 May 2020, updated 22 July 2024. Supports: grief is natural; signs that someone needs professional help include struggling to function day to day, hopelessness, and a wish for death or preoccupation with it.

title: Quran 2:180: Making a will
label: Quran source
note: Cited for: making a will for parents and close family is prescribed when death approaches. Classical scholars read it together with the inheritance verses 4:11 and 4:12. The English wording is a translation of the meaning, from The Clear Quran (Dr. Mustafa Khattab), the Quran.com default.

title: Quran 4:11: The fixed inheritance shares
label: Quran source
note: Cited for: the fixed shares of inheritance, which are divided 'after the fulfilment of bequests and debts'. The English wording is a translation of the meaning, from The Clear Quran (Dr. Mustafa Khattab), the Quran.com default.

title: Sahih al-Bukhari 2742: One third, and even one third is a lot
label: Hadith reference
note: In Sahih al-Bukhari (Book 55, Hadith 5). Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas asked to bequeath his wealth and the Prophet allowed 'one third, yet even one third is too much'. Cited for: a bequest is limited to one third of the estate.

title: Wills and Powers of Attorney Guided Pathways
label: Public rights source
note: Supports: a free Ontario online tool that creates a simple will and powers of attorney. It is not legal advice, and it suggests seeing a lawyer.

title: Think about making a dependant's support claim
label: Public rights source
note: Reviewed 19 December 2025. Supports, for Ontario: a dependant the person supported (a spouse, former spouse, child, stepchild, grandchild, parent, grandparent or sibling) can ask a court for support from the estate, usually within 6 months of an estate trustee being named.

title: Think about choosing an equalization payment
label: Public rights source
note: Reviewed 19 December 2025. Supports, for Ontario: a married spouse chooses either what the will or the intestacy rules give, or an equalization payment under family law, and must ask the court for an equalization payment within 6 months of the death.

title: Sahih al-Bukhari 6764: Inheritance across religion
label: Hadith reference
note: In Sahih al-Bukhari (Book 85, Hadith 41), narrated by Usama ibn Zayd: 'A Muslim cannot be the heir of a disbeliever, nor can a disbeliever be the heir of a Muslim.' The basis of the majority view.

title: Sahih Muslim 1614: Inheritance across religion
label: Hadith reference
note: In Sahih Muslim (Book 23, Hadith 1), with the same wording as Sahih al-Bukhari 6764.

title: A Muslim inheriting from a non-belligerent non-Muslim (Fatwa 189195)
label: Scholar answer
note: 1 November 2012. Supports: the majority, including the four schools, allow no inheritance across religion; a minority (including Mu'adh ibn Jabal, Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab and Ibn Taymiyyah) let a Muslim inherit from a non-Muslim who is not hostile; a will from a non-Muslim to a Muslim is valid like any other bequest.

title: FCNA Guidelines on Fostering and Guardianship
organization: Fiqh Council of North America with AMJA (Zainab Alwani)
label: Scholar answer
note: 7 November 2021, updated 13 August 2026. Supports: fostering and guardianship (kafalah) are praised; keep the child's biological family name as a last or middle name; mahram rules after puberty; breastfeeding before age two creates mahram status; a special bequest of up to one third for a child in kafalah, more if the heirs permit. The page calls the five-feedings rule unanimous, but the schools differ on the number. Written for Muslims in the United States.

title: Quran 9:113: Asking forgiveness for polytheists
label: Quran source
note: Cited for: it is not proper to seek forgiveness for polytheists, even close relatives, 'after it has become clear' that they are bound for the Fire. Verse 9:114 explains Abraham's prayer for his father. Scholars explain its scope, so the site cites it only together with their answers. The English wording is a translation of the meaning, from The Clear Quran (Dr. Mustafa Khattab), the Quran.com default.

title: Quran 17:15: No punishment before a messenger is sent
label: Quran source
note: Cited for: Allah does not punish a people until He has sent a messenger to them. The English wording is a translation of the meaning, from The Clear Quran (Dr. Mustafa Khattab), the Quran.com default.

title: Sahih al-Bukhari 2937: A prayer for the guidance of Daws
label: Hadith reference
note: In Sahih al-Bukhari. When the tribe of Daws refused Islam and he was asked to curse them, the Prophet prayed for their guidance instead. Cited for: praying for the guidance of living family.

title: The Fate of Non-Muslims: Perspectives on Salvation Outside of Islam
label: Scholar answer
note: Published 7 March 2018, updated 14 January 2026. Supports: the main traditional view that Islam is the accepted religion, held together with Quran 17:15 that no one is punished before a messenger reaches them; al-Ghazali's standard that a person must hear about Islam reliably and accurately; restraint in judging any individual's fate. The paper also reports wider views that are not the site's position.

title: Praying for forgiveness for a deceased non-Muslim parent (Fatwa 5934)
label: Scholar answer
note: 24 July 2013, answering a convert about his father. Supports: Quran 9:113 applies only where a person's fate in the Fire is certain; someone who did not receive the message properly may be excused, so a child may ask Allah to forgive a parent in that position.

title: How to Deal With a Non-Muslim Relative's Death
label: Scholar answer
note: 23 May 2011. Supports: while a relative is alive, pray that Allah puts faith in their heart; after death you do not formally pray for forgiveness for them, but it is permissible to hope that Allah created faith in their heart.

title: What Is the Proper Etiquette in Giving Condolences to the Family of a Deceased Who Is Non-Muslim?
label: Scholar answer
note: 2 November 2015, checked by Shaykh Faraz Rabbani. Supports: customary condolences are fine; do not ask forgiveness for the deceased (9:113), but you may ask that they receive what is best and leave the matter to Allah.

title: Can You Expand on What to Do When a Muslim Baby Is Born?
label: Scholar answer
note: 5 October 2023. Supports, in the Shafi'i school: the call to prayer in the right ear and the iqamah in the left, putting a softened date in the baby's mouth (tahnik), naming, shaving the head and giving charity on the seventh day, and the aqiqah as a confirmed sunnah. Whispering the baby's name is not an established sunnah.

title: Sunan Abi Dawud 5105: The call to prayer in a newborn's ear
label: Hadith reference
note: In Sunan Abi Dawud, graded Hasan by Al-Albani on Sunnah.com. The Prophet gave the call to prayer in the ear of al-Hasan when he was born. The strength of this report is debated; see Jami' at-Tirmidhi 1514.

title: Jami' at-Tirmidhi 1514: The call to prayer in a newborn's ear
label: Hadith reference
note: In Jami' at-Tirmidhi. At-Tirmidhi called it hasan sahih, while Sunnah.com shows the grading Da'if (Darussalam). Cited to show that the strength of the report is debated.

title: Rulings on Aqiqah (Fatwa 81462)
label: Scholar answer
note: 7 January 2001. Supports: the aqiqah is a confirmed sunnah for those who can afford it; two sheep for a boy and one for a girl, on the seventh day, otherwise the fourteenth or twenty-first, or any time before puberty.

title: Circumcision of baby boys: Information for parents
label: Public health source
note: Last updated February 2021. Supports: the CPS does not recommend routine circumcision of every newborn boy; parents often choose it for religious, social or cultural reasons; a trained, experienced practitioner should do it with a local anaesthetic; no provincial or territorial plan pays for circumcision done for non-medical reasons. The CPS position statement the handout links to has been retired.

title: First-of-their-kind guidelines for mood and anxiety disorders in pregnancy and postpartum
label: Public health source
note: 12 February 2025. Supports: 23% of mothers who recently gave birth in Canada reported feelings consistent with postpartum depression or an anxiety disorder (a figure from the Survey on Maternal Health, 2018/2019); new clinical guidelines and a patient guide exist.

title: Spiritual Care
label: Public health source
note: One hospital, as an example: spiritual care is requested through the care team; prayer rooms at two campuses are open 24/7; Muslim prayers on Fridays at 1 p.m.

title: Immunization Vaccine (Fatwa 84728)
label: Scholar answer
note: 19 June 2011. Supports: avoid gelatin in food, and in medicine too unless there is no alternative, in which case it may be taken; lists the reasons (a mixture, a tiny amount, injection, transformation) and says this matches the OIC Fiqh Academy.

title: Organ Donation and Blood Transfusion (Fatwa 76781)
label: Scholar answer
note: 5 November 2008. A short answer from one scholar: donating organs or blood is allowed whatever the religion of the donor or recipient, except to a specific recipient who shows open hatred of Islam.

title: Residents' Bill of Rights: your rights if you live in a long-term care home
label: Public rights source
note: February 2025, under the Fixing Long-Term Care Act, 2021. Supports, for Ontario: right 10, to pursue social, cultural, religious and spiritual interests with reasonable help; right 16, to accommodation, nutrition, care and services consistent with the resident's needs.

title: Choosing a substitute decision maker
organization: Canadian Hospice Palliative Care Association (Speak Up)
label: Public health source
note: 8 May 2025. Supports: a substitute decision maker makes health decisions when you cannot; the legal names for this role differ across provinces and territories; your support network can include spiritual leaders.

title: What is the Islamic view on ending life support?
organization: Fiqh Council of North America (Shaykh Mustafa Umar)
label: Scholar answer
note: 16 November 2022, updated 13 August 2026. Supports: euthanasia is forbidden; treatment that only prolongs dying is not required, including life support, respirators and feeding tubes, after expert medical advice and consultation.

title: Medical assistance in dying (MAID)
label: Public health source
note: Modified 27 August 2025. Supports: the request cannot be the result of outside pressure; a person can withdraw the request at any time and in any manner; federal law does not force anyone to provide or help provide MAID; a person whose only condition is a mental illness is not eligible until 17 March 2027.

title: On Organ Donation and Transplantation
organization: Fiqh Council of North America (Dr. Jasser Auda and Dr. Jamal Badawi, reviewed by Dr. Aasim Padela)
label: Scholar answer
note: 6 October 2021, updated 13 August 2026. Supports: donation is permissible in principle, with no sale, the donor's informed consent and family consultation; out of caution FCNA does not include brain death in the definition of death, so donation after death waits for the heart and breathing to stop; donating reproductive organs is prohibited.

title: Fatwa on Organ Donation (1881)
label: Scholar answer
note: 14 August 2006. The answer quotes the resolution of the Islamic Fiqh Council of the Muslim World League: donation from the deceased is allowed if the donor gave permission before death and the recipient's life depends on it; living donation must not harm the donor. It says nothing about brain death.

title: Deceased donation
label: Public health source
note: Supports: register your intent to donate and tell your family; 'your loved ones must give consent to honour your wishes'. This does not describe Nova Scotia, which uses deemed consent.

title: Organ and tissue donation registries
label: Public health source
note: Supports: links to the donor registry or method of each province and territory listed on the page (Nunavut is not listed).

title: Organ and tissue donation
label: Public health source
note: Opened on 25 September 2026. Supports: in Nova Scotia, if you are 19 or over and do not register a decision, you are seen as having consented to donate under the Human Organ and Tissue Donation Act (deemed consent), with listed exceptions.

title: Deaf Muslims of Canada
label: Community organisation
note: Supports: organisers can book ASL interpreters for events through DMC, which also trains interpreters in Islamic signs. The site footer shows 2025. Charity status and religious orientation are not stated on the page.

title: About ISDHH
organization: Islamic Services for the Deaf and Hard of Hearing
label: Community organisation
note: A United States (Texas) nonprofit. Supports: ASL classes, ASL interpretation of the Friday khutbah, and prophet stories in ASL.

title: Sahih al-Bukhari 6307: Seeking forgiveness more than seventy times a day
label: Hadith reference
note: Sahih al-Bukhari 6307 (Abu Hurairah), in Sahih al-Bukhari: the Prophet said he asked Allah's forgiveness and turned to Him more than seventy times a day. Supports the glossary entry for istighfar and astaghfirullah as a daily phrase.

title: Quran 98:5: Worship Allah with sincere devotion
label: Quran source
note: Quran 98:5 says people were commanded to worship Allah, sincerely devoting their faith to Him. Supports the glossary entry for ikhlas (sincerity).

title: Sahih al-Bukhari 52: The lawful and the unlawful are clear, with doubtful things between
label: Hadith reference
note: Sahih al-Bukhari 52 (An-Nu'man bin Bashir), in Sahih al-Bukhari: the lawful and the unlawful are evident, between them are doubtful things, and whoever keeps away from them protects their religion and honour. Supports the glossary entry for mashbooh (doubtful).

title: Quran 2:168: Eat what is lawful and good
label: Quran source
note: Quran 2:168 (The Clear Quran): 'O humanity! Eat from what is lawful and good on the earth.' Supports the glossary entry for tayyib (good and wholesome) alongside halal.

title: Sahih al-Bukhari 756: No prayer without Al-Fatihah
label: Hadith reference
note: Sahih al-Bukhari 756 (Ubada bin As-Samit), in Sahih al-Bukhari: 'Whoever does not recite Al-Fatiha in his prayer, his prayer is invalid.' Supports the glossary entry for Al-Fatihah as part of every prayer.

title: Quran 4:86: Return a greeting with a better one or the same
label: Quran source
note: Quran 4:86 (The Clear Quran): when you are greeted, respond with a better greeting or at least similarly. Supports answering the salam with the same words or fuller ones.

title: Sunan Abi Dawud 5195: The fuller forms of the salam
label: Hadith reference
note: Sunan Abi Dawud 5195 (Imran ibn Husayn), graded Sahih by al-Albani: As-salamu alaykum earns ten, adding wa rahmatullah twenty, and adding wa barakatuh thirty. Supports the fuller greeting and reply.

title: Quran 18:23-24: Say 'if Allah wills' about future plans
label: Quran source
note: Quran 18:23-24 (The Clear Quran): never say of anything 'I will definitely do this tomorrow' without adding 'if Allah so wills'. Supports saying in sha Allah about plans.

title: What Is the Etiquette of Using 'In Sha Allah'?
label: Scholar answer
note: Shaykh Yusuf Weltch, checked by Shaykh Faraz Rabbani, citing Quran 18:23-24 and Tafsir Ibn Kathir: saying in sha Allah about future intentions is recommended, and if you forget you say it when you remember.

title: Quran 18:39: 'What Allah has willed'
label: Quran source
note: Quran 18:39 (The Clear Quran): 'This is what Allah has willed! There is no power except with Allah!' The source of ma sha Allah, la quwwata illa billah on seeing something good.

title: Sahih al-Bukhari 6224: What to say when someone sneezes
label: Hadith reference
note: Sahih al-Bukhari 6224 (Abu Huraira), in Sahih al-Bukhari: the one who sneezes says Alhamdulillah, the one who hears says Yarhamuk Allah, and the first replies Yahdikumullah wa yuslih balakum.

title: Jami at-Tirmidhi 2035: 'May Allah reward you with good'
label: Hadith reference
note: Jami at-Tirmidhi 2035 (Usamah bin Zaid), graded Hasan (Darussalam): whoever is done a favour and says 'May Allah reward you with good' has praised in the fullest way. Supports Jazak Allahu khayran as a thank-you.

title: Sunan Abi Dawud 2130: Congratulating a newly married person
label: Hadith reference
note: Sunan Abi Dawud 2130 (Abu Hurayrah), graded Sahih by al-Albani: the Prophet congratulated a man on his marriage with 'Barak Allahu laka wa baraka alayka wa jama'a baynakuma fi khayr'.

title: Sahih al-Bukhari 780: Say Ameen when the imam says it
label: Hadith reference
note: Sahih al-Bukhari 780 (Abu Huraira), in Sahih al-Bukhari: say Ameen when the imam says it after Al-Fatihah. The text is about praying behind an imam; it does not cover praying alone or how loudly to say it.

title: Sahih Muslim 410a: Say Ameen when the imam says Ameen
label: Hadith reference
note: Sahih Muslim 410a (Abu Huraira), in Sahih Muslim: 'Say Amin when the Imam says Amin', and whoever's Amin matches that of the angels is forgiven past sins. About praying behind an imam.

title: Sahih al-Bukhari 1284: Words of comfort to the grieving
label: Hadith reference
note: Sahih al-Bukhari 1284 (Usama bin Zaid), in Sahih al-Bukhari: the Prophet sent word to his daughter, whose child was dying, that whatever Allah takes and gives is His, everything has a fixed term, so be patient and hope for reward. He wept and called his tears mercy.

title: Sahih al-Bukhari 3616: What to say when visiting the sick
label: Hadith reference
note: Sahih al-Bukhari 3616 (Ibn Abbas), in Sahih al-Bukhari: when visiting a sick person the Prophet said 'la ba's, tahurun in sha Allah'. Sunnah.com's English renders it 'No harm will befall you! May Allah cure you!'; the Arabic word tahur means purification.

title: Jami at-Tirmidhi 3443: Farewell words for a traveller
label: Hadith reference
note: Jami at-Tirmidhi 3443 (Salim, from Ibn Umar), graded Hasan (Darussalam): the Prophet bid travellers farewell with 'Astawdi'ullaha dinaka wa amanataka wa khawatima amalik'.

title: What Are the Etiquettes of Eid? (IslamQA 36442)
label: Scholar answer
note: Section 4, offering congratulations: any good wording is fine, such as Taqabbal Allahu minna wa minkum or Eid mubarak. It reports that the Companions greeted each other with 'May Allah accept from us and from you', and that Ibn Hajar graded the chain hasan (Fath al-Bari 2/446). IslamQA follows one school of thought.

title: Quran 33:56: Send blessings and peace on the Prophet
label: Quran source
note: Quran 33:56: believers are told to invoke blessings and peace on the Prophet. The basis for saying sallallahu alayhi wa sallam (peace be upon him).

title: Jami at-Tirmidhi 3546: The stingy person does not send blessings
label: Hadith reference
note: Jami at-Tirmidhi 3546 (Ali): 'The stingy person is the one before whom I am mentioned and he does not send salat upon me.' Sunnah.com shows no Darussalam grade; at-Tirmidhi's own verdict in the Arabic text is hasan sahih gharib.

title: Sahih al-Bukhari 636: Pray what you catch and complete what you missed
label: Hadith reference
note: Sahih al-Bukhari 636 (Abu Huraira), in Sahih al-Bukhari: on hearing the iqamah, walk to the prayer calmly, pray what you catch with the imam and complete what you missed. The basis of the term masbuq.

title: Sahih al-Bukhari 605: The wording of the adhan and the iqamah
label: Hadith reference
note: Sahih al-Bukhari 605 (Anas), in Sahih al-Bukhari: Bilal said the adhan phrases twice and the iqamah phrases once, except qad qamatis-salah. It gives the wording of the iqamah, not its timing.

title: Sunan Abi Dawud 695: Pray close to a sutrah
label: Hadith reference
note: Sunan Abi Dawud 695, graded Sahih by al-Albani: when you pray facing a barrier (sutrah), keep close to it.

title: Sahih al-Bukhari 1549: The words of the talbiyah
label: Hadith reference
note: Sahih al-Bukhari 1549, in Sahih al-Bukhari: the wording of the talbiyah the Prophet said in ihram, beginning Labbayk Allahumma labbayk.

title: Sahih al-Bukhari 5472: The aqiqah for a newborn
label: Hadith reference
note: Sahih al-Bukhari 5472 (Salman bin Amir), in Sahih al-Bukhari: 'Aqiqa is to be offered for a newly born boy.' The text names a boy; details for boys and girls are for a teacher.

title: Sahih Muslim 2985: Deeds done for someone besides Allah
label: Hadith reference
note: Sahih Muslim 2985 (Abu Huraira, hadith qudsi), in Sahih Muslim: whoever does a deed associating someone else with Allah in it is left with that partner. The basis for warning against riya (showing off).

title: Sahih al-Bukhari 1264: The Prophet was shrouded in three white cloths
label: Hadith reference
note: Sahih al-Bukhari 1264 (Aisha), in Sahih al-Bukhari: the Prophet was shrouded in three white cotton cloths. Supports the glossary entry for kafan.

title: Sahih al-Bukhari 150: Washing with water after the toilet
label: Hadith reference
note: Sahih al-Bukhari 150 (Anas bin Malik), in Sahih al-Bukhari: a container of water was taken for the Prophet when he went to relieve himself, so he could wash. Supports the glossary entry for istinja.

title: Quran 3:159: Put your trust in Allah
label: Quran source
note: Quran 3:159: consult with people, and once you have made a decision, put your trust in Allah. Supports the glossary entry for tawakkul (trust in Allah after taking the means).

title: Quran 23:100: A barrier until the Day of Resurrection
label: Quran source
note: Quran 23:100 speaks of a barrier (barzakh) behind the dead until the Day they are resurrected. Supports the glossary entry for barzakh.

title: Quran 17:79: Prayer in part of the night
label: Quran source
note: Quran 17:79 tells the Prophet to pray tahajjud in part of the night as an extra prayer. Supports the glossary entry for tahajjud.

title: Quran 2:158: Safa and Marwah
label: Quran source
note: Quran 2:158: Safa and Marwah are among the symbols of Allah, and pilgrims may walk between them. Supports the glossary entry for sa'i.

title: Quran 22:36: The sacrificial animals
label: Quran source
note: Quran 22:36 describes the sacrificial camels as symbols of Allah and says to eat from them and feed the needy. Supports the glossary entry for udhiyah (qurbani).

title: Quran 5:89: The expiation for a broken oath
label: Quran source
note: Quran 5:89 sets the expiation for breaking a deliberate oath: feeding or clothing ten poor people or freeing a slave, and if that is not possible, fasting three days. Supports the glossary entry for kaffarah.

title: Quran 17:1: The Night Journey
label: Quran source
note: Quran 17:1 describes Allah taking His servant by night from the Sacred Mosque to the Farthest Mosque. Supports the glossary entry for Isra and Mi'raj.

title: Quran 107:6: Those who only show off
label: Quran source
note: Quran 107:6 speaks of those who pray only to be seen. Supports the glossary entry for riya (showing off in worship).

title: Quran 91:9: Whoever purifies the soul
label: Quran source
note: Quran 91:9: successful is the one who purifies the soul. Supports the glossary entry for nafs (the self).

title: Quran 2:228: The waiting period after divorce
label: Quran source
note: Quran 2:228 (The Clear Quran): 'Divorced women must wait three monthly cycles before they can re-marry.' Supports the glossary entry for iddah.

title: IJMES Transliteration System for Arabic, Persian and Turkish
organization: International Journal of Middle East Studies (Cambridge University Press)
label: Transliteration chart
note: The standard academic chart for writing Arabic letters in Latin script: th for one letter, dh for another, a dotted z for a third, q for qaf and a mark for the letter ayn. Supports the glossary's point that plain English spelling merges different Arabic letters. It says nothing about stress.

title: Quran 9:100: Allah is pleased with them
label: Quran source
note: Quran 9:100 says of the first Emigrants and Helpers: 'Allah is pleased with them and they are pleased with Him.' The wording behind radiyallahu anhu (RA), said after the Companions.

title: Is It Appropriate to Use Abbreviations Like SAW and SWT?
label: Scholar answer
note: Answered by Mufti Muhammad ibn Adam (Darul Iftaa Leicester), 2009. Quotes Imam al-Nawawi (Sharh Sahih Muslim 1.39) that writing the full blessing is recommended, and calls abbreviations inappropriate. One mufti's answer; it does not cover RA or AS.

title: What do all these titles mean? (Qalam Institute)
label: Seminary page
note: A US Sunni seminary's own usage: shaykh or shaykha for a graduate of higher Islamic study with years of teaching and community work; mufti for a graduate licensed to give fatwas; ustadh or ustadha for a graduate beginning to teach, or a certified specialist; imam for a graduate serving as a community's imam. The page says it does not dictate any other institute's titles.

title: The Shaykh and the Ustadh Defined
label: Article
note: Guest post by Abdul Wahab Saleem (2014). Describes how titles such as shaykh, alim and ustadh are used loosely in Western Muslim communities, sometimes for age or activism rather than training. An opinion piece, used alongside the Qalam Institute page.

title: Mispronunciation of the Fatiha
label: Scholar answer
note: Checked by Shaykh Faraz Rabbani, 2020. Quotes Reliance of the Traveller f18.8 (Shafi'i): a letter mistake spoils that word, which is said again correctly, but the prayer is only invalid when the mistake changes the meaning and was deliberate. Advises fixing the word once, ignoring waswasa and learning with a teacher.

title: Is My Prayer Valid If I Mispronounce Saad as Seen? (Hanafi)
label: Scholar answer
note: Shaykh Faraz Rabbani, citing Ibn Abidin's Radd al-Muhtar: mixing up saad and seen by accident does not invalidate the prayer, because it is a widespread difficulty, and the learner should make a reasonable effort to learn.

title: Quran 73:4: Recite the Quran in a measured way
label: Quran source
note: Quran 73:4 (The Clear Quran): 'recite the Quran properly in a measured way'. The basis for learning careful recitation (tartil) over time.

title: Quran 56:79: Touched only by the purified
label: Quran source
note: Quran 56:79. The Clear Quran renders it 'touched by none except the purified [angels]'. Scholars read the verse in different ways, which is part of why they differ on touching the mushaf without wudu.

title: Could We Touch Quran Without Wudu (AMJA fatwa 82276)
organization: Assembly of Muslim Jurists of America (AMJA)
label: Scholar answer
note: The four imams do not allow touching the mushaf without wudu; al-Hasan al-Basri, Ibn Sirin and Ibn Hazm allowed it. The mufti finds the permissive view stronger and will not call it prohibited, but advises having wudu as the safer course.

title: How Was the Prohibition on Touching the Quran (Even Translation) without Wudu Derived?
label: Scholar answer
note: Mawlana Ilyas Patel: the Hanafi school counts a translation as Quran in meaning, so wudu is needed to touch it. The Shafi'i, Maliki and Hanbali schools allow touching a translation without wudu (citing al-Majmu' and al-Mughni).

title: Quran Software Application and Entering the Toilet
label: Scholar answer
note: Checked by Shaykh Faraz Rabbani, citing Tahtawi (Hanafi): close the Quran app and keep the phone in a pocket before entering the toilet, and do not touch the verses on the screen without wudu.

title: How Does One Dispose of an Unused Quran?
label: Scholar answer
note: Shaykh Yusuf Weltch, checked by Shaykh Faraz Rabbani, 2020, citing Ibn Abidin: first consider keeping it, giving it to a masjid or gifting it. Otherwise bury it, Arabic or translation, where no one walks; shredding is also allowed.

title: Rulings Related to Disposal of the Mushaf (Islamweb fatwa 510508)
label: Scholar answer
note: A damaged cover is no reason to dispose of a copy. Pages that can no longer be read may be buried or burned to protect them, citing Uthman's order in Sahih al-Bukhari.

title: Sahih al-Bukhari 4987: Uthman's compilation of the Quran
label: Hadith reference
note: Sahih al-Bukhari 4987, in Sahih al-Bukhari: after the standard copies were made, Uthman ordered all other written Quranic materials to be burnt. The precedent for burning unreadable pages respectfully.

title: Quran 74:4 - Purify your garments
label: Quran reference
note: 'And purify your garments' (Al-Muddaththir 74:4). The basis for keeping clothes clean for worship.

title: Sahih al-Bukhari 220 - Pouring water over urine on the floor
label: Hadith reference
note: Sahih al-Bukhari 220 (Abu Hurairah): when a Bedouin urinated in the masjid, the Prophet told the companions to pour a bucket of water over it and said 'You have been sent to make things easy'. Sahih.

title: Sahih al-Bukhari 227 - Menstrual blood on clothes
label: Hadith reference
note: Sahih al-Bukhari 227 (Asma'): menstrual blood on a garment is rubbed, washed and rinsed with water, then she can pray in it. Sahih.

title: Sahih al-Bukhari 223 - A milk-fed baby boy's urine
label: Hadith reference
note: Sahih al-Bukhari 223 (Umm Qais): the Prophet poured water over the urine of a baby boy who had not yet eaten food and did not wash it. Sahih.

title: Sahih Muslim 279a - A vessel licked by a dog
label: Hadith reference
note: Sahih Muslim 279a (Abu Hurairah): if a dog licks a vessel, its contents are thrown away and it is washed seven times. Sahih. Washing once with earth appears in other narrations, not in this one.

title: What Distinguishes the Cleaning Process Between Light and Moderate Filth? (Shafi'i)
label: Scholar answer
note: Shaykh Irshaad Sedick, 24 September 2023. Shafi'i: heavy filth (dog, pig) is washed seven times, one with earth; light filth (urine of a milk-fed boy under two) is sprinkled; other filth is washed until its substance, colour and smell are gone where feasible.

title: Finding Filth on Clothing After Prayer (Hanafi)
label: Scholar answer
note: Ustadh Tabraze Azam, checked by Shaykh Faraz Rabbani, 11 July 2012. Small marks in underwear found after the prayer that were not there at wudu: do not repeat the prayer, because events are ascribed to the nearest possible time. Narrow: it does not cover every stain found later.

title: How Much Filth Is Excused in the Shafi'i School?
label: Scholar answer
note: Ustadha Shazia Ahmad, 26 December 2022, citing Reliance of the Traveller f4.3 to f4.4. Excused: filth too small for ordinary sight, one's own blood or pus whether much or little, and a little blood or pus from someone else.

title: How Do I Wash My Clothes Properly to Ensure That Filth Doesn't Spread? (Hanafi)
label: Scholar answer
note: Ustadha Sulma Badrudduja, checked by Shaykh Faraz Rabbani, 9 February 2011. Clothes that come out of a washing machine free of any trace of filth may be taken as pure; pre-wash the soiled spot.

title: Can We Use Deodorants, Creams, and Perfumes That Contain Alcohol? (Hanafi)
label: Scholar answer
note: Shaykh Faraz Rabbani, 25 June 2011. Non-wine alcohol is not ritually impure and may be used externally; avoiding it is more precautious because of the difference of opinion, including a stricter view within the Hanafi school.
